 The First Fury represents personal and domestic forms of mental suffering and anguish.
 Cp. Aeschylus, Eumenides 246: τετραυματισμένον γὰρ ώσ κύων νεβρὸν/πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σταλαγμὸν
ἐκματεύομεν (‘we track as a dog tracks a wounded fawn, following the dripping blood’); and Twelfth
Night I i 21–3: ‘That instant was I turn’d into a hart,/And my desires, like fell and cruel hounds,/E’er
since pursue me’. S.’s lines, like Shakespeare’s, evoke the myth of Actaeon, the hunter who was turned
into a deer by the goddess Artemis and hunted down by his own hounds in punishment for having
seen her naked while bathing. S. also alludes to the story in Epipsychidion 272–4, and Adonais 274–9.
 GM noted that lake seems a curious word in this context, and that brake would make much better
sense; but lake is clear in Nbk 7.

paragraphs.source_en:
Second Fury
465 The beauty of delight makes lovers glad,
Gazing on one another: so are we.
 As from the rose which the pale priestess kneels
To gather for her festal crown of flowers
The aerial crimson falls, flushing her cheek,
470 So from our victim’s destined agony
The shade which is our form invests us round,
Else are we shapeless as our mother Night.
